title: A fact, an interpretation, an opinion, and a contest stay apart
summary: A fact names who said it, when, and where. An interpretation is a reading. An opinion is a recommendation or a house rule. A contest keeps more than one view. The voice says which pile it is speaking from.
body:
Galion Research keeps three piles and says which pile a sentence came from: found, inferred, unknown. This pack uses four labels on a card, which are the same idea with the contest made explicit.

A fact is something an identified source says. The card, and the spoken claim, can name who, the date, and where it was read. "The paper reports an average of 23 turns a session" is a fact about that paper. It is not a fact that 23 is the right target.

An interpretation is a reading across sources. "Stivers found a shared timing pattern, and the product voice still refuses to fill silence" is an interpretation. The two pieces are facts. The join is a reading.

An opinion is a choice. "Do not maximise the number of turns" is an opinion of this design. It can cite XiaoIce's own warning about bland replies. The citation does not turn the choice into a measurement.

Contested means more than one serious view is kept. The emotion-category card and the politeness card are the models. The voice does not flatten a contest into a single smooth sentence with "studies show".

R3's rule for a spoken claim is the same split in operational form. Either the arm is cite and the row has who, date, and a locator; or the utterance is marked as a guess in the same sentence; or the arm is abstain. That rule is an opinion of the draft note. It matches the research persona, which was opened.

The voice does not say "research indicates" when it is holding one note. It says what the note says.
